utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Mr. Sterc. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. That is that you will speak the truth, whole truth and nothing but the truth. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sterc. I'd like to refer to your evidence on Wednesday, where you gave evidence that your view that the extent of the devastation and lack of infrastructure after Operation Storm made it impossible for anyone to return to the area in August and September, that that was based on your conclusions as an outside observer, and I believe you referred specifically to newspaper articles. And I'd like to direct you to another portion of your statement, which is in paragraph 9.1 where you stated that the unorganized and unplanned moving in after Operation Storm by a large number of displaced person who had lost their homes practically couldn't have been prevented." And, first, by "displaced persons," you're referring there to Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question completely, I did not say explicitly that all -- any movement was impossible and that people did not return. However, they did not return in an organised manner. As to your question, my answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And your statement that this unorganized and unplanned moving in of these displaced persons practically couldn't have been prevented, in relation to the time-period before you became assistant minister in October, is that also based on your observations as an outside observer to the events?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the following. This was not exclusively about the returnees. This is about all the people who had to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina under the given circumstances. They crossed the Sava river at Davor and entered Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if could you just answer my question. Is this observation based on what you perceived as an outside observer in relation to the time-period before you became assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't object to the question; however, it was part of her question that these were displaced persons, and I believe the witness was answering that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness is now invited to complete his answer so that he fully answers the question of Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A newspaper wrote about that and you could see it daily on TV. You could see columns of people from Bosnia-Herzegovina headed for Croatia as a result of the departure from -- for -- of Serbs from Croatia and then entering Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Danube area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, you're referring here -- the columns of people from Bosnia, these are -- headed for Croatia, these are also Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could please turn Exhibit P463, and in particular, page 9 in English and page 14 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, this is a record of a meeting between Minister Radic and President Tudjman on the 22nd of August, 1995, so before you joined the ministry. And I'd like to just read you a passage and ask you a couple of questions. And if we go to the bottom of the English of that page, Mr. Radic says: "Now, look, have I been looking around this area a bit, the biggest centres where we should focus on return, regarding the national interest, I have tried to make a chronological order or some kind of hierarchy, and in my opinion, I would like to discuss this with you a bit." "The map of the whole area is of a strategic importance for Croatia. I coloured it with different colours. This is what has always been critical for us in the history, not Knin, we'll manage to do that slowly."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "If you ask me the first -- I define five priorities according to the urgency of colonising these places with Croats. If you ask me, this thing right here is the first and the second priority. We should bring Croats back here urgently and this area should be urgently colonized with Croats, and we should by no means let no more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here again because that's where we got cut off." And the president says: "Not even 10 per cent?" And Mr. Radic says: "Okay. I'm talking about 10 per cent, so the first priority of colonising is this right here in my opinion, Petrova and Zrinska Gora. That's where we have to establish some kind of a city sooner or later. We also have Vojnic and Veljun, a somewhat smaller place, but Vojnic is a bigger place. "However, by our companies, opening factories, just as the Serbs did in Licki Osijek, I visited that factory. That looks marvellous. They built apartments for 4.000 people, where we can bring people right away. It's just that we don't have anybody, somewhere in this area we must build ..." And the president says: "That has been preserved too?" And Radic says: "Everything has been preserved, completely wonderfully preserved." My first question to you is, were you aware that Mr. Radic had defined five priorities according to the urgency of colonising these places with Croats?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And these areas that Radic refers to as the first priority, Petrova Gora and Zrinska Gora. These areas in general included the municipalities of Vojnic, Vrgin Most, Glina, Petrinja, Kostajnica, and Davor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And before the war in 1991, these -- this was an area that was largely populated by ethnic Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the municipality. The Serbs did not prevail in all of the municipalities that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in Vojnic, they were about 90 per cent; is that right? Vrgin Most about 70?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Glina about 60?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Petrinja about 45 per cent?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Kostajnica about 62 per cent. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry have I been asked to repeat my question. Kostajnica was about 62 per cent Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the town of Kostajnica or the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The municipality.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Davor was about 85 per cent Serb, that municipality?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, I'll remind you that on Wednesday you said you were -- your observations on the extent of devastation and lack of infrastructure at this time in August and September, that was based on your views as an outside observer. And you can see here that Mr. Radic points to an area where he says they can bring people in right away and says it has been wonderfully preserved. If the minister of reconstruction and development took the view at this time that the situation in an area was such that people could be brought in right away, you wouldn't have any reason to doubt that, would you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched TV, and I did not see that those areas were that well preserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But here Mr. Radic says that he was visited that factory that looks marvellous. Do you have any reason to doubt his conclusion as to the state of this factory in Licki Osijek?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that he did visit Licki Osijek and that he did observe what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to confirm something you said on Wednesday. You -- you testified that you didn't know Mr. Radic before you were appointed, and I just want to make sure I understand exactly that you went by that. Before you joined the Ministry of Reconstruction on the 11th October 1995, have you ever spoken with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were members of the Council for Demographic Development and Reconstructions, and as a member of that council, I came to the meetings but we never actually talked. We did not know each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you never had a one-on-one conversation with Mr. Radic before the 11th of October, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meetings encompassed all scientists dealing with similar issues, primarily demographic issues. We had several meetings, several general discussions, but we did not have any particular conversations about anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we turn now to 65 ter 4628, in particular page 11 of the English and page 20 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, this is a record of another meeting between Mr. Radic and President Tudjman, and this one was on the 12th of September, 1995. And if you see about three sentences into Mr. Radic's statement there, he says: "We have to tactical this problem. We also have a problem with the expelled people, all of them, after Operation Oluja, and have the data from the 1991 census. There were 123.000 residential units in the liberated area, 123.000 flats and houses, and there are 120.000 Croats that we want to return to the area, which means one house to each Croat (yes). This means that this business of return, which we started before the reconstruction, must be accelerated, either through legislation or by employing other measures, because there is not a single family that we cannot provide accommodation for. We have enough houses. "Now, since we do not have damage estimates, it's a bottleneck, because my experts need to go out in the field with engineers, et cetera ... between 30 per cent and 35 per cent of the 123.000 is either completely destroyed or heavily damaged, so it won't do. But there are still some 80.000 houses and flats, which again, I think, is terrible. Of that number, 16.000 are state-owned or socially-owned, or owned by the railway company, which virtually means state-owned. It is it a huge potential for highly-skilled people and returnees from abroad, and that is my principal motive for raising this question. I believe that the time is ripe for you to issue a declaration ... the emigres ..." If we could turn the page in the B/C/S? "Therefore, I could perhaps furnish you with some background information. But I think we have to, this would be a crucial invitation. What can we offer them? The current number of returnees is way too small, way too small for populating the area. The latest information I is that along with those moving from Banja Luka, some 10.000 will soon come from Vojvodina. They are even headed for Subotica and even for ... however, half of those who arrive either run away or simply disappear. They are afraid or, I don't know, to accept, tentatively speaking, a Serbian house, and they prefer to stay with ... relatives or some other persons, or they disappear among the tenants living in rented flats in Zagreb or elsewhere. On the other hand, we have been sending out several invitations a week to highly skilled people willing to come and live in these new areas, to come forward, and the response was fantastic, really fantastic. We have received approximately 12.000 applications for settling in the area." Now, Mr. Sterc, were you aware that Radic had taken these steps to accelerate the population of the area with Croats by, for example, sending out these invitations to people to settle these areas.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the conversation, and I did not know about any of those actions that were undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to page 17 of the English and page 25 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, I'd like to direct your attention to the top of this page, about halfway through Mr. Radic's statement, he says: "We have to reinforce this department in the ministry because I have no one in charge of the settlement. I have talked to two persons. I need an assistant in that ministry of that level, for the spatial strategy. I don't know if you know Sterc. He used to work in the institute for applied social research. He was the youngest at the institute, and he agreed. I asked him if he would like to be an assistant and he agreed. He is efficient, rather temperamental, a youngish man, perhaps two to three years my junior." Now, Mr. Radic is talking about you here, isn't he, when he says Sterc; that's you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is thinking about me but he didn't even know I was working. I wasn't working in the institute for applied social investigations -- applied social research.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here he says that he had asked you if you would like to be an assistant, and you agreed. Do you remember Mr. Radic asking if you wanted to be assistant minister around this time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So when I asked you earlier if you'd ever had a one-on-one conversation with Mr. Radic, and you said no, you did have a conversation, didn't you? You had a conversation with him about your appointment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for some foundation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But this wasn't a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I -- I don't think the impeachment is complete. I don't think she has laid the foundation for the -- I mean, I don't want to say it in front of the witness, but ... the question posed was was it one-on-one. The second question is was he offered an assistant minister post. She hasn't establish that the second took place under the conditions as in the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just re-reading the previous answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, in answer to my earlier question about having a one-on-one conversation with Mr. Radic before the 11th of October, 1995, you said no. And then you said -- you went on to say "we did not have any particular conversations about anything." Did you in fact have a particular conversation with Mr. Radic about your appointment as assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer this question. It wasn't an tete-a-tete conversation, and we didn't specifically discuss the kind of work that was to be performed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When I asked you if it was right that Mr. Radic had asked you if you wanted to be assistant minister around this time, you said yes. What exactly were the circumstances in which Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- asked you to become assistant minister and you said yes. Tell me about that conversation.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some members of the ministry for development and reconstruction were present at the conversation, the secretary and I don't know who else, and it was very brief. It wasn't possible during that period of time to speak at length with the ministers who were supposedly big fish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could just finally turn to page 4 of this second English translation of this document, and page 30 in the B/C/S. And it's at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Dr. Radic here is talking again about you. And he says: "Yes, Klemencic accepted it immediately. They are also from the council of demography. He worked all the time there, both he and Sterc, and Klemencic is a bit meticulous and Sterc is more operational. So I've thought of Sterc. The two of them were assigned as follows; Sterc as assistant and the other one as counsellor precisely to study a strategy of that, and of operational programme and let them be there until the time for that come." And if we move down to the -- skip the next paragraph and move down to the following one. He says: "Secondly, the Law on Strategy of Croatian Space - that is a working title. So, which areas are to be stimulated, especially in term of settlement, which to be exempt from taxes, which were not, everything equal, simply define, and Sterc, Klemencic, and those over there, and we are almost finished. I think that is something representing a strategic law." And here Mr. Radic refers to you in connection with a proposed Law on Strategy of Croatian Space dealing with the areas to be stimulated, especially in terms of settlement. Is this something that you had worked on before you joined the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object now. Prosecution objected to paragraph 5 of the statement. It was excluded based on her objection. Now she's going into the area on cross when I was precluded from going into it on direct. So I'm going to object to this line of questioning because it's unfair that we were precluded on the basis of her claim that she was prejudiced by paragraph 5 and now she's going into that topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- it's not clear to me, at least, that this is the same topic, and, secondly, it's a purely factual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I too thought it was a purely factual question which the basis why I asked that paragraph 5 be admitted and I be allowed to explore paragraph 5 and it was excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not entirely, Mr. Misetic. Those portions that were purely factual, the Chamber said you can make up your mind. It's 5.5, 5.6, 5.7 that is where the statement talks about not an analysis of -- of the publications, et cetera, but where it is about the programmes that were developed and what they contained, what chapters would be in those programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well I may go into it then in redirect, Mr. President, if I'm allowed, but if the -- given the connotation that's being ascribed to the programme in cross, then I may wish to explore paragraphs 5.1 -- at least the factual basis for paragraphs 5.1 through 5.4, because it's now been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said at the time that those paragraphs are not fit for being admitted under Rule 92 ter. If you want to explore purely factual matters in which the issues are dealt with on a factual basis, there seems to be no problem, and I think the Chamber has never kept you off from putting factual questions. I think the reasoning was -- at least I thought our ruling was clear on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, I'll just repeat my question because it was a few minutes ago. Mr. Radic here refers to you in connection with the proposed Law on Strategy of Croatian Space dealing with the areas to be stimulated, especially in terms of settlement. Is this something that you had worked on before you joined the ministry?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why Mr. Radic might have referred to you in connection -- in mentioning this law?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he referred to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to another topic, and this is the property law measures that are discussed at some length in your statement. This is paragraph 9 and 9.1 and 9.2. And in paragraph 9.1, you refer to the Law on the Temporary Takeover and Administration of Property. And you state that this was not confiscation of property as it was perceived, rather, at the time it was felt that this property need to be protected from destruction or secured if it was occupied by tenants. And my first question is you weren't involved in drafting or in any way in the creation of this law, were you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And as you point out in your statement it was passed in September 1995 before you were appointed assistant minister. Do you know anything at all about how this law came to be drafted or enacted?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I assume that lawyers drafted this law, worked on this lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence of a meeting held on 11th August 1995 with President Tudjman and other senior members of the Croatian leadership, including Dr. Radic, Mr. Susak, Mr. Granic, and Mr. Valentic, among other, at which they discussed the purpose and the terms of this law which was then in the parliamentary process, and I'm referring here to P462. Do you know anything about that meeting or what was said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the views of any of those individuals I just mentioned, about the purpose of this property law?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So when you talk in your statement about this law being -- about protecting property from destruction, would it be fair to say that that's more or less your personal view, that you can't speak for the top Croatian leadership as to the purpose of this law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about the meaning of the law in the field on site. After we had formed the assembly -- the council when we saw what the law meant for the actions that we subsequently planned. So these are matters that I can address.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you know, then, that the law -- put the property of the Serbs who had left the Krajina into the temporary possession of the state and only gave those Serbs 90 days to return and reclaim their property. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked about this. I asked lawyers about this before I came here because I believed that would be a question put to me, and all the lawyers said that that 30-day-time limit isn't something that can be found in the law, isn't stipulated in the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In fact, this law is in evidence, and it does provide for a 90-day period. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everyone who worked on that told me that this 30-day limit isn't in the law. But this is just hearsay information, so I can't saying anything about that. I can just talk about the consequences of the law and what it meant for us when we started dealing with the entire concept of returning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any confusion about the 90 days and the 30 days. It's my -- is my recollection right that there was a draft which mentioned 30 days and that then 90 days were adopted, and this went back to discussion in late August 1995, if I remember well. If that is the case, perhaps we should perhaps put it to the witness, because he is talking about the 30 days and you're talking about the 90 days, so that upon apparent agreement between the parties - and I'm just now referring to Mr. Misetic nodding - yes, I don't remember the details under what circumstances the 30 days became 90 days. I know that there was a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I may, I believe -- I don't have the exhibit number at my fingertips, but I believe there was a government decree that provided for 30 days passed on the 31st of August and then there was a later law that changed that to 90 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties assist in -- Mr. Misetic do you have...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was an initial government decree that didn't have the power of a parliamentary law, that is correct. That was then passed as a law at 90 days and then amended again in January of 1996 to have no limitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sterc, were you able to follow the exchange of views between Chamber, Prosecution, and Defence, in this respect that initially there was a presidential decree which stated that the time-limit would be 30 days, that then a law was adopted, which, at least from what I understand was valid during 1995, once it was adopted, and that it was later changed. So when we're talking about 30 days, there apparently was a presidential decree which stated that the time-limit for return was 30 days, in order not -- in order to avoid the consequences described in that law, to apply, whereas that was later changed or -- was not changed but a law was adopted which mentioned 90 days. Ms. Gustafson, any questions in this respect, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, did you ever read this law that was passed in September 1997 on the temporary takeover of property about which you have given evidence in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's 1995, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you read that law, Mr. Sterc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the opportunity to read it, but I didn't. And to clarify this misunderstanding that has arisen, lawyers tell me, or told me before I came here, that all the time-limits with regard to the law had to do with the Law on Selling Flats for which tenants had right. But there was no time-limit for regaining one's property. That's all I can say. Unfortunately, I'm not informed of all the detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you answer the question on the basis of your own knowledge and not on what others told you, unless you clearly indicate that, and that law is in evidence. We have discussed it and the time-limits - and the parties will correct me if I'm wrong - time-limits do appear also in legislation which was not exclusively dealing with tenants' rights of apartments. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And perhaps then we could turn to that topic, which is tenants' rights. And you discuss this in paragraph 9 and 9.2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honours, I apologise, I neglected to tender the transcript we looked at which was 65 ter 4628. Could that please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there are no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to 65 ter 3496, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, I'd like to direct your attention to the title, the Law on the Lease of Flats in the Liberated Territory, which is near the bottom of the first column. Are you familiar with this law?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at Article 1 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "This law regulates the leasing of flats for which, in accordance with provisions of this law, the tenants' right terminates over publicly owned property, state-owned property, i.e., property owned by legal entities who acquired this ownership on the grounds of special regulations and are located on the formerly occupied, now liberated territories of the Republic of Croatia." Now, this law, Mr. Sterc, that was enacted on the 27th September 1995, this law dealt exclusively with tenants' rights in regards to flats that were located in the territories taken over after Operations Storm and flash; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "The tenants' rights over flats defined in Article 1 of this Law terminates by lawful force --" I think it reads, "if the bearer of the tenants' right has abandoned the flat and has not used it for a period longer than 90 days since the day this Law came into force." And if we go down to Article 3, it says that: "The flats ... under this law which are leased by" your minister, "the Ministry of Development and Reconstruction." And if we go to Article 4, which is on the next page in the English, sets out the categories of people to whom the ministry can lease these flats. And if we go to Article 8, which, again, is on the next page in English, and the next page in the B/C/S as well. And this states that the person who is -- leased this flat by the ministry has the right to buy the flat under certain circumstances. Now, basically, Mr. Sterc, this law extinguished the tenancy rights of the Krajina Serbs to socially owned property if they failed to return to those flats within 90 days of the date this law was enacted, the 27th of September, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand this, it applies to everybody who resided in the areas that had been occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And those people lost their tenancy rights if they failed to return within 90 days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All those who had resided in that area, according to the 1991 census, and I'm talking about the area that had previously been occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you discussed property laws relevant to tenants' rights in connection with the departure of Serbs during and after Operation Storm. And, again, that's paragraph 9 and paragraph 9.2. And the law that you specifically referred to was the Law on Sale of Flats in Tenancy, a 1992 law that was amended several times. When you discussed the rights of tenants in connection with the departure of Serbs during and after Operation Storm, why didn't you mention this law here?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have any reason. I thought that we're talking about a law --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, could you slow down your speed of speech, because the interpreters have difficulties in following you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Sterc. Can finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be instructed to repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that, according to my assumption, that was one of the modifications of the law and the dead-lines were moved because these people were provided time to ask for the right to purchase their apartments. The apartment that they had tenancy rights to. But I'm talking about all the people from the area, not only the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said according to your assumption there was one of the modifications of the law. But this is a different law, right? This Law on Lease of Flats in the Liberated Territories is a different law from the Law on Sale of Flats in Tenancy; right? I see you nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I apologise. This was one of the derivations of that law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You say it's a derivation of that law --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my assumption. I don't know that for a fact. Because I'm not a lawyer. I am not able to use the same terms equally well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 9.2, you refer to tenants' rights and negotiations. You state: "Negotiations regarding tenants' rights were long and intensive." Now, here are you talking about negotiations with the international community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And these were negotiations about the mechanisms as to whether and, if so, how, Serbs would be allowed back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Serbs, but everybody to their original homes, in Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this law here, the Law on the Lease of Flats in the Liberated Territory, that was a law that was a particular concern to representatives of international organisations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that one. We discussed all the laws. Even the previous one, we discussed it, and I never provided my final position as to why I provided the statement I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your last answer. Your final position as to what -- what statement?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that all the laws were discussed, all the laws that were passed by the Republic of Croatia, or, rather, the Croatian parliament. There were also discussions at our meetings of the Working Group, not about the return of the Serbs but everybody to their homes, and we discussed all the laws that needed to be amended, changed, or improved, not only in Croatia but also in the other parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit D419, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, this --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, if I could tender the property law -- the Law on the Sale of Lease of Flats in Tenancy, 65 ter 3496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the document that's coming up now, Mr. Sterc, is an OSCE report from the 8th of September, 1998, and you were referred to it, I believe, in your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to paragraph 26. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It says: "The resolution of property issues remains crucial to the advancement of the return process, the establishment of trust and postwar normalisation. As called for in our May Progress Report, Croatia has taken some positive steps in this regard. Parliament has rescinded the 1995 Law on Temporary takeover of Specified Property ... and the 1995 Law on Lease of Apartments in the Liberated Areas, both of which had discriminatory effects and contravened international commitments. The mission had repeatedly called for the recision of these laws." Mr. Sterc does that more or less accurately describe the concerns that representatives of the international institutions expressed about these laws to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was discussed, but this is it not a realistic presentation of the situation, atmosphere, procedures, and results of the work undertaken by the Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understood your answer in connection with my question, which was whether this accurately represented the concerns that representatives of international organisation expressed to you about these laws.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was concern, but this does not reflect the real situation that we discussed and were -- were able to finally agree upon at the Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 7343 please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, these are minutes of a Croatian government session from the 14th of September, 1995, a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 11 in the English, and page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you see the comments of the president of the government, Mr. Valentic. He says: "Item 1 is a very important issue, draft Bill on the lease of flats in the liberated area, along with the final draft Bill [sic]." And then he asks the deputy prime minister, Bosiljko Misetic to give an explanation, and you see --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, I think we're on the wrong page in the B/C/S. If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S, at the bottom of that page. Oh, I apologise, that was the correct page, it was just at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So here we are. This is right now, the comments of Mr. Bosiljko Misetic, and he says: "After the military and police reintegration of the occupied areas, with the aim of the most rapid possible reconstruction, return and the Croatian people populating the liberated areas, there is, among other, a great number of flats in these now liberated areas which have, until recently, been occupied." And if we could go to page 12 in the English and the next page -- or at the bottom of the current page in B/C/S. It says: "What is important is there have been proposals of handling those flats in such a way whereby they would be given directly into ownership, but out of the reasons why we had and the manner in which we have regulated in the bill on the sequester, it would not be purposeful for them to be given immediately into ownership, this also due to abuses. "In addition --" and I think if question go to the next page in the B/C/S. "In addition we believe that we are additionally encouraging people with the solutions offered who will come, use the flats as lessees, stay on in these areas, which would be a long-term demographic and economic and every other Croatian objective. The lease would amount to the same as the rent. After a certain period of time leasing the flat the lessee would be entitled, I stress again, under privileged conditions, in accordance with the law in force, to buy this flat from the state and gain ownership of it."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go now to page 14 in the English and page 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you see Mr. Radic speaks. He says: "I think that we should quite certainly take this law as an integral whole with the decree, that is, the Law on the Allocation of Houses, which had been in private ownership to date, because with both one and the other we intend to and must resolve the shortages, people in the liberated area, in particular, so that of the skilled personnel, and that is why I propose that the possibility of those same commissions doing the allocation of both those houses and these flats be looked into. They have been similarly, almost identically formed ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, finally, if we go to page 17 in the English and page 20 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These are further comments of Mr. Bosiljko Misetic. And at the second paragraph he says: "The purpose of this law is primarily the reconstruction and return to those areas. That is why Mr. Petrovic's proposal, the immigration minister, should both be supported and recognition should be lent to it; this, moreover in a way that all those institution, all institutions and all ministries, when adopting their programmes of return, primarily take into account, both in view of employment and return, that this is for the immigrants, that is to say, Croatian immigration or the Croatian diaspora, however one labels it." And in the next page in both the English and B/C/S he says: "The purpose of the law is therein, primarily the return, economic, and demographic recovery." Now, Mr. Sterc, I take it you were not aware of this government session at which this law was discussed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if could I tender that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to another topic, Mr. Sterc, which is the agreement of the Joint Working Group that you discussed in paragraph 13 of your statement. And you gave evidence about this as well on Wednesday. And in your testimony you said that: "It was just one of the steps we made to deal with the whole situation in order to implement our design of the return of everyone to their homes." That was at transcript page 20316. And I'd just like to clarify one point on this agreement with you, which is with respect to mechanisms for return. And this agreement only set out procedures for a two-way return into and out of Sector East. In other words, it set out mechanisms for displaced Croats to return to Sector East; and for displaced Serbs who were living in Sector East to return to other parts of Croatia, if that is where their homes were; is that right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is not about displaced Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, didn't this agreement provide mechanisms for Croats from Eastern Slavonia to return to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the intention of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the time this agreement was made, in April of 1997, there were no corresponding procedures for return for the much larger number of Serbs from the Krajina who were living outside Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no former document, but there were talks and there were procedures aimed at return, until the moment a document could be formalised.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that formal document that provided mechanisms for Serbs outside of Croatia to return, that was the programme enacted in June of 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the final document following all the other preceding documents that we had done in drafting much before they were actually signed and dated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on Wednesday, Mr. Misetic asked you about the reasons why Serbs left Eastern Slavonia between August 1996 and July 1998, and you testified that you thought the main reasons were political and economic uncertainty there. Now, regardless of those reasons, the Croatian leadership was encouraging the departure of Serbs from Eastern Slavonia and viewed their departure as positive. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian government was not in control of Eastern Slavonia. Everybody knows that. 18.000 Serbs who had left, the rest of the occupied territory of Croatia ended up in Eastern Slavonia, according to our estimate. In order for Croats to come back to the UNTAES territory, we had to implement the concept of return of everybody to their homes. I really don't know, nor was I ever complained -- or heard complaints about international -- from the international community that Croatian state encouraged the departure of Serbs from Eastern Slavonia to some other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, the question was not whether anyone complained about what the Croatian state encouraged or did not encourage. It was one step back; that is, quite simple, whether the Croatian leadership was encouraging the departure of Serbs; and, second part of the question, whether they viewed their departure as positive. Could you please answer that question, not on whether it was criticised or not. Perhaps that may be the next question. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would have a Rule 90(H) objection on this question. Ms. Gustafson cross-examined Ms. Skare Ozbolt and these questions were not put to her, who would have had personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to slow down. It's virtually impossible to interpret simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before Ms. Gustafson responds, Mr. Sterc there is a repeated request that you slow down your speed of speech if you want us to here your testimony, but I do understand that you're missing the guidance of Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will try to take over now and then with my hand signals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I don't think there is any reason I shouldn't be able to put this to the witness he has given evidence about reasons for the departure of Serbs. I'd like to test foundations of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, my -- she can test it but to the extent we're going develop the issue further, the reason we bring persons with personal knowledge is to have these issues addressed directly with people with personal knowledge and not that -- then a subsequent witness comes who doesn't have personal knowledge and then we start trying to admit documents on a particular topic. So I would have a 90(H) objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is on the record. Ms. Gustafson may proceed and we'll see at the end whether we enter into the Rule 90(H) areas, yes or no. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to go a document next that would take a few minutes, so perhaps the Chamber would be prefer to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps it's better to first have a break. We'll have a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00. But not until I've asked you, Ms. Gustafson, how much further time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour to 45 minutes Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take it that we'll certainly be able to conclude the evidence of this witness this morning. And, for the record, Mr. Misetic is nodding yes. We have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, I'm going to repeat my last question because I don't think we ever got an answer to it, which was that the Croatian -- that the Croatian leadership encouraged the departure of Serbs from Eastern Slavonia and viewed their departure as positive; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we please go to 65 ter 7252.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, this is a transcript of a meeting of the VONS held on 17th December at -- 1996. And are you familiar with the VONS, the Defence and National Security Council of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could stay on this page in the English and move in the B/C/S to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You see President Tudjman asks the meeting to go on to the next item in the agenda, which is report in the course of the reintegration in Podunavlje. And Podunavlje, that's another term for Eastern Slavonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although it's not quite identical, but I don't have time to go into explanations that concern such geographical concepts now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you see, then, Dr. Ivica Kostovic speaks and part way down that speech he says: "The first issue is the treatment of Serbs by the Croatian authorities, starting from the government all the way to the mayor who comes into direct contact with them, while the second issue are the elections. I will tell you what is to be done with regards to the issue of the treatment of Serbs. First of all, --" And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S, please. "First of all, full protection should be given to the two or three Serbs who we are going to encounter in Baranja, as was the case in Nijemci and when we entered Srijem triangle. That kind of protection cannot be undertaken. Instead, there ought to be a practical change in the policy of the local authorities of all who are going to go there. "Furthermore, in Baranja, UNTAES does not allow us..." And then the President says --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "What does it mean, why, what?" And Dr. Kostovic says: "Here is an example: There were 47 Serbs in Nijemci. First, we stalled issuing them documents and this and that. Then, we offered them everything and all of them left, save Jovanka. Jovanka remained there and Budby wrote to the Security Council about her, as initially she did not get the documents on time and then people came to her and threatened here. And so without Klein, now Budby speaks of the return of the Jordanian battalion to those ... and that is the truth, I am not joking, that is what is happening. So, because of a single Serb woman, I cannot keep what I have won with great effort - Srijem triangle. It is because of this that, for example, a meeting of county prefects should simply be called and they should be told, You are state officials, and whenever any of your people enter any of those settlements which Klein had given you, and if you do not protection, you will be replaced. And that should, for example, be told to the county prefects, they in turn will pass it on to the mayors and that is it. I cannot risk the process of peaceful reintegration on the account of a single Serb woman." And President Tudjman says: "Right, that's understood, someone even needs to be replaced. However, let it be clear that this is not -- let it be, I did this ... but as a part of this."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Kostovic responds: "Yes, that's true. But that we point that out for ourselves as well ... I do not want that. In Baranja, only four families are in the chasm, and if I cannot pay them off, bribe them, to go away to who knows where, and if that is the price of entering Baranja, then I am neither the Croatian state nor the authority. There, that is approximately that message." And then he goes on and says: "The second thing that needs to be done - and the prime minister has already given the green light for it - is the simple compensation, meaning that we would pay off the Serbs, and that is somewhere between 30 and 50 per cent, those who live around Vukovar, that is more than 50 per cent, Bilja, while those who live in Baranja are, let's say, 30 per cent. That is some kind of statistical data which was obtained. That ought to be the responsibility of the office for the refugees and the local authorities. They need to find Croats who will buy those half-destroyed houses of theirs."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to the next page in English: "Our bank would give a loan to a Croat, he would give that money to a Serb, and the Serb would sign he would not return there anymore. The Americans are all crazy about that. And so, if everyone is crazy about it, let us do so." And if we can go to one further page which is at page 13 of the English and page 18 in the B/C/S. And this is Dr. Radic speaking. And if we go to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, he says: "Third, the Serbs are the most corrupt people in the world. There isn't a single more corrupt or purchasable nation. Starting from this fact, I believe that we can achieve much more, as we just said, by buying their property, for which we have created a good ... I believe that the matter can proceed well through the weekend houses, around there. But, I believe we shall be able to achieve what we need to do in that space. Since recently I have spoken quite often to their representatives, who occasionally visit Zagreb, et cetera. Stanimirovic and the others, they are amazed at the fact that, I mean, in individual meetings with them - but, you need to assign people to do the job, and they will be able to do quite a lot."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, do you know about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you don't know anything about the comments made by members of the leadership about bribing Serbs in Eastern Slavonia to go away or buying their houses in order to -- as Radic said, "achieve what we need to do in that space." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that when I asked you about whether the Croatian leadership was encouraging the departure of Serbs from Eastern Slavonia and viewed it as a positive development, that you can't really speak about those views of the top Croatian leadership, about that issue. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I can speak about that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 65 ter 7252.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe if we can check the interpretation, I believe it was page 35, line 21, if we can check what the witness's answer was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said: Naturally I can speak about that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if he can speak about it perhaps we should ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sterc, I misunderstood the answer. You said you can speak about the views of the top Croatian leadership, but you said you didn't know anything about the meeting or the comments made by the leadership about bribing Serbs in --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like you, if you could please explain how you reconcile those two remarks?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to be allowed to be a little bit more precise when answering questions, because my "yes" and "no" answer do not reflect the situation and the information I had about this matter when we discussed the matter with representatives of the international community. Would the chamber allow me to give somewhat a lengthy answer because in previous conversations, when discussing the issue of tenancy rights, I didn't have the opportunity of explaining what we negotiated on, what sort of agreements we reached with regard to tenancy -- the tenancy agreement issue which was discussed with international community. As far as this matter is concerned, and as far as I'm concerned, the people who are referred to here can say whatever they like. You mentioned Mr. Kostovic. For example, Mr. Kostovic was the -- was the deputy prime minister, but he wasn't someone who could in any way issue orders to me. To act as he saw fit in Podunavlje, that's what you call it, I was present with UNTAES every week. I would see them every week that, included President Klein, Deputy Srdarijan [phoen] and others, Piper, Campbell and so on and so forth. We discussed various actions that I mentioned the day before yesterday -- yes, thank you. And apart from what they thought, well, I can also tell you what my opinion is, this seems to me as if it's young children playing at war. Pressure through the formal bodies and the agreements that we had wasn't at public sessions -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You really have to speak more slowly, otherwise we'll miss your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what this Chamber wishes to happen. Please slowly proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, there were weekly negotiations with UNTAES, and during those negotiations we tried to reach agreements, according to which the Serbs who had left the previously occupied territory and who had come to Podunavlje could remain in Podunavlje, in Croatian buildings, while the process of returning wasn't placed within a framework --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm go to interrupt you, because I don't believe you've addressed my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object. She asked him if he knew the views of the Croatian leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and now he starts explaining what happened on the ground which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- starting to get after two days some facts about what the witness may now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- to explain what the position of the Croatian leadership was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Sterc, at the end of your testimony you can add anything which you consider not to have been dealt with sufficiently; of course, within certain limits. You've told us quite a bit about your dealings with the international community. Ms. Gustafson, at this moment, is apparently exploring to what extent you were aware of what -- or in what atmosphere the matter was dealt with at meetings with the presidents -- with the president, and that's what she refers to if you're talking about the leadership. If you could give us a further insight, not primarily on what happened on the ground, because I think you told us already that your efforts were aiming at guaranteeing the right of everyone to return if that person had left, it being a humanitarian issue. But Ms. Gustafson, at this moment, is apparently exploring what you could tell us about these view, as she read them to you, which were aired in these meetings with the president. If you say, Well, I consider this a schoolboys' meeting, then, of course, that -- I wouldn't say so, but at least we have, at this moment, no reason to believe that it was just schoolboys' conversation. If you would like to give us a better insight on what happened there, which seems to be not fully consistent with your own views on the matter, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A direct answer with regard to what they discussed, there is nothing I can say -- I can't provide any details about what they discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender 65 ter 7252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We object. We object to the admission of this document, Ms. Skare Ozbolt is listed as having been present for the meeting, under Rule 90(H) it should have been put to her. I note that the final question was, You weren't present so you don't know anything about the views of the views of the Croatian leadership. We had Ms. Skare Ozbolt here who could have, perhaps, provided some answers to that. So to that extent I would object and say that it's improper to not put it to Ms. Skare Ozbolt and then wait for a witness who doesn't know anything about the meeting and then tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, Rule 90(H) doesn't require us put any particular document to a witness. It requires us to put the general nature of our case. We certainly put the general nature of our case on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. 90(H) and 98 are easily confused. I see on the transcript that Mr. Misetic was understood to refer to 90(H), although from what I thought and also in view of his earlier observation, that it would be 98 or is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 90(H) okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that has been, at least any confusion in my mind, is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh I'm not finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we first ask Ms. Gustafson to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We certainly put our case to Ms. Skare Ozbolt on the views of the leadership with respect to the -- the presence or absence of Serbs in Eastern Slavonia. Furthermore, the fact that we didn't put that to her shouldn't be a bar to putting to this witness to test his knowledge of those views. And, lastly, Your Honour, if we had unlimited time to put documents to witnesses, might have put this document to Ms. Skare Ozbolt. We have to make discussions as to what to focus on. With regard to that witness, we focussed on the focus of her testimony on this issue which was the negotiations that led up to the Erdut Agreement. And we put those documents to her. So I don't think the objection is warranted for that reason. And the fact that no one who was present at this meeting has testified in this case should -- is a matter that should go to the weight that the Chamber assigns to it, not its admission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would remind the Chamber that when this issue came up with Mr. Rajcic, we had to go through an entire procedure of calling Mr. Rajcic back because a document was put to a different witness and he had to be re-called for that purpose. Now, the difference being that the document that we tendered through that -- a different witness later wasn't Mr. Rajcic's own document. He didn't participate in any meeting. He had no firsthand knowledge of that document. Nevertheless, he was required to be re-called to address that document. This is a situation that's even more -- I think, clear, in that Ms. Skare Ozbolt is actually present at the meeting. I would also note that in her statement, which is now in evidence -- I believe it is paragraph 7 of her statement. If I can find the D number. D1471 at page 7 she said: "During the peaceful integration of Eastern Slavonia when I would receive information that the Serbs wanted to leave a certain area, I would personally go into -- go to the area in order to negotiate with them in order for them to remain in the area." Now, it was put in issue, it was clearly flagged for the Prosecution that that was an issue with respect to her testimony. If we use the Rajcic example where he had to be re-called about a document that he wasn't the author of and had no firsthand knowledge of, then here in this case I think -- certainly in the worse case scenario, the same procedure should be applied, and I think it should be excluded because clearly this should have been put to her. Whether it's top -- or this particular document or more importantly the general topic of what Ms. Skare Ozbolt said in her statement, even that wasn't addressed with her regardless of the specific document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the last 30 seconds for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's just that the comparison with the Rajcic document isn't an apposite one, Your Honour. These matters depend on the nature of the document. Most of the presidential transcripts have been admitted from the bar table by both parties. They're documents that are suitable to admission from the bar table. It's not necessary to have a witness who has personal knowledge of the document for them to be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. I'm just trying to get a better impression on the presence and the participation of Ms. Skare Ozbolt in this meeting, which I find on page 11. The document will be -- will be marked for identification. Both parties will have an opportunity to make further submissions on this issue, not later than Monday, close of business. And the parties are then invited to give exact references on what was dealt with, where, and what pages, et cetera. Parties are also invited to consider whether it is a matter which goes to admissibility only or whether a re-call of Ms. Skare Ozbolt would be a remedy under the circumstances. Not to say that the Chamber has formed any opinion about whether there's anything to be remedied, but, nevertheless, the Chamber would invite the parties, that in case there would be, then to see to what extent this would be a remedy. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to ask is it, do we have 3.000 words or is it less?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no. I would say if would you start with two pages or two and a half pages, and if there's a clear matter you say, This issue needs another ten page, indicate there, and then the Chamber will consider whether those other ten pages will be allowed, yes or no. If we have not received anything by Monday, close of business, then, of course, the Chamber will proceed to consider the matter on the basis of the oral submissions. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit number is P2593, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will keep that status for the time being. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, I'd like to move on now to the Programme for Return that you discussed in your statement that was passed in -- or enacted in June of 1998. And my question is this. There was a great deal of pressure placed on Croatia and the Croatian leadership to enact mechanisms to allow the return of Serbs to Croatia and to ensure its effective implementation; isn't that right? And I mean -- by "pressure," I mean pressure from the international community.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There were pressures from the international community from the very outset for all of our moves, the moves of the Croatian government, and, of course, there was a lengthy discussion about that. The programme of return was preceded by several documents that were signed with the international community, and the return was the Crown of a concept of everybody's return to their homes. Since I did not have the opportunity to say the following, and I believe that this is important, let me say this. When it comes to the programme of return which was coordinated with all the representatives of the international community or the leading people thereof in Croatia, that programme defines the right of tenancy over the apartments, and this is defined very clearly, unambiguously with the conclusions and co-signatures by everybody. The tenancy rights was on the agenda and was the subject of a lengthy discussion, and this was the key document of the entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to go to 65 ter 7344 and page 59 of the English and the third attached translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, this is a report of the non-governmental organisation, Human Rights Watch, from March of 1999, and I'd like to direct your attention to the passage under the title, "The European Union." Where it says: "Closer integration into so-called Euro-Atlantic structures, including European Union and NATO, are key elements of Croatian foreign policy. The European Union, therefore, plays an influential role in Croatia. EU relations with Croatia are governed by the Union's regional approach to countries of South East Europe which conditions granting of trade concessions, reconstruction assistance, and other relations with all countries in the region on a comprehensive set of human rights criteria, including the creation of conditions for the return of refugees and displaced persons and respect for the rights of minorities." And then it goes on to refer to a six-month review done by the EU council of ministers. And in the next paragraph it says: "At the last review in October 1998, the council decided that relations should remain unchanged, citing a discrepancy between statements of intent and their practical implementation, as well as problems with respect to the treatment of minorities and a very slow return process. Croatia currently enjoys autonomous trade measures with the EU but was suspended from the fair reconstruction assistance programme soon after it originally became eligible in 1995 due to the military actions Storm and Flash." And if we skip to the following sentences: "The threat by the EU to suspend ATMs is widely regarded as instrumental in the decision of the Croatian government to adopt the mandatory instructions for the procedure on individual return in May and the return programme in July." And if we go to the next page in the English, and the next page in the B/C/S, I believe, as well, under the United States: "The United States maintains a close relationship with Croatia." And then if we go down, a few lines down it says: "The US has indicated a willingness to support Croatia's admission to the NATO partnership for peace programme, provided that progress can be made on refugee returns, Dayton implementation, and internal democracy." Is that passage consistent with your understanding of the types of pressures placed on Croatia and the Croatian leadership to enact and implement a programme to return Serb refugees to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't look like pressure to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it says here: "The threat by the EU to suspend ATMs is widely regarded as instrumental in the decision of the Croatian government to adopt the mandatory instructions in May and the return programme in July?" Are you saying that that doesn't seem like pressure to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can explain. On the previous page, you see a threat that the reconstruction conference on Croatia will be put on hold. That conference was held at Westin hotel in Zagreb. All the high representatives of the international community attended. I personally attended the conference and delivered a speech there. Similar threats which included the introduction of functions for Croatia were heard during the conversation when the programme was being adopted. And one more sentence, please, this will allow to understand the whole situation. At one point after all such pressure, I spoke to the representatives of the international community and told them, Okay, as of tomorrow, please impose sanctions on Croatia, although I did not even know how the Croatian government would react to that, although I was a member of that same government. After half an hour break, we reached agreement on all points as if there hadn't been any threats prior to that. What I'm saying is this is my experience. I'm talking from experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So just to go back to one part of your answer. You talked about the threat of sanctions. There were threats of sanctions on Croatia in relation to the return of Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, your question is not very precise. It applied to everybody's return to their homes and the adoption of the programme. The position was that we didn't wanted the Croats from Bosnia to return to Bosnia. And I repeat what our position was: Our position was the return of everybody to their own homes, because that was the only solution to the complicated situation in the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And these threats of sanctions by the EU and pressure by the United States, that created a dilemma for the leadership, didn't it, because while the leadership wanted to integrate into these structures and benefit from that integration, they did not want to allow for the return of Serbs to Croatia which was one of the conditions of that integration, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't understand your question. I apologise. I really did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise. The question was that these international pressures created a dilemma for the Croatian leadership, because on the one hand they wanted to integrate into EU and into NATO, and, on the other hand they did not want to allow for the return of Serbs to Croatia, which was one of the conditions of integration; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no dilemma present at the Croatian government. At that moment, fortunately -- or unfortunately, as you will, I was the one who represented the Croatian authorities as the president of the Working Group. And, of course, we all knew that the threats were only rhetorical.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There were discussions by representatives of EU and EU institutions and the United States and the leadership in Croatia that took place at a much higher level than you, right, on this issue?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I was not interested in that higher level, and I don't know what was discussed at that higher level. I only know what our interest was, what the interest of the international community was, and we wanted to bring that matter to an end.
